parts:
Dear all, 

Quasi-complete separation often occurs in data sets that I work with. I typically deal with it by using the blme package. For example, for this dataset at the end of this post, I use the model below:

summary(bglmer(y ~ cond1 + (1|item) + (1|subject), data = data, family="binomial",  fixef.prior = normal(cov = diag(9,2))))

And it works pretty well.  I wonder how I can do something similar in Stan. My current Stan model is below. However, the output is pretty bad (e.g., small effective n, large SEs of beta)). I wonder how I can impose a weakly informative prior in order to resolve the separation problem. Thanks!


model.stan <- 'data {
int<lower=1> N;
int<lower=1> NS;
int<lower=1> NI;
int<lower=1, upper=NS> subject[N];
int<lower=1, upper=NI> item[N];
vector[N] cond1;
int y[N];
}

parameters {
vector[2] beta;
real u[NS];
real w[NI];
real<lower=0> tau_u;
real<lower=0> tau_w;
}
model{
beta ~ normal(1, 1000);
tau_u ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001); 
tau_w ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001); 
u ~ normal(0, sqrt(tau_u));
w ~ normal(0, sqrt(tau_w));

for(i in 1:N){
   y[i] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(beta[1] + u[subject[i]] + w[item[i]] + beta[2]*cond1[i]));
}
}
'

Hi Xiao,

In general, it's best to try to tighten priors when you're having N_eff problems. See section 5.2 of the manual, specifically advice on "uninformative" proper priors. For example, using a scale of 1000 for the beta priors is likely too large, as is the scale on your tau_w and tau_u.

Also, looking to the manual for ideas about reparameterization is also helpful. See the section 19 in the manual. The trick to getting better results for your model came from the transformation you'll see in the transformed parameters block, just as on page 180 of the manual. The new model is attached. Play around with the scale for the priors on beta and you can see how this affects your inferences for beta. Note that the normal density in Stan is parameterized by the standard deviation, rather than the variance.


Rob

Xiao:
See my 2006 paper.  In short, never never inv_gamma(0.001,0.001).  Better to just do uniform.  Better still to use some weak prior info on the tau’s.  Also, parameterize the sd’s, not the variances.  Finally, for the regression coefficients, use soemthing stronger than normal(1,1000).  You could do N(0,10), which probably is still too broad but would probably be a better default start.
A

Xiao:
See my 2006 paper.  In short, never never inv_gamma(0.001,0.001).  Better to just do uniform.  Better still to use some weak prior info on the tau’s.  Also, parameterize the sd’s, not the variances.  Finally, for the regression coefficients, use soemthing stronger than normal(1,1000).  You could do N(0,10), which probably is still too broad but would probably be a better default start.

Quasi-complete separation often occurs in data sets that I work with. I typically deal with it by using the blme package. For example, for this dataset at the end of this post, I use the model below:
